\section{Conclusion}\label{sec:7}\ThesisCheckNumber{section}{7}

This thesis examined the association between water and sanitation conditions and child anthropometric outcomes in four Sub-Saharan African countries: Ethiopia, Ghana, Kenya and Nigeria. Two distinctions ran throughout: household facilities versus surrounding community WASH, and a single survey-date exposure versus a preliminary, geospatially matched measure of modelled local WASH coverage during the child's early-life window, built for an earlier survey round in three of the four countries, with Ethiopia retained only as a provisional sensitivity analysis (Section 1.4).

The baseline evidence shows no clear, robust association between improved household WASH and child outcomes when households are compared within the same DHS cluster (Section 5.1): inconclusive, not evidence of no association. The community measure shows a large, significant unadjusted association for most outcome/exposure pairs, attenuating to non-significance once socioeconomic status and region fixed effects are added (Section 5.2), consistent with, though not proof of, confounding by local development.

The historical extension links earlier DHS rounds from Ghana, Kenya and Nigeria to IHME's modelled annual local WASH coverage for a defined early-life window (Sections 3.5, 6.5). Its headline cell, the pooled established-date water--HAZ association, is positive and significant, independently reconstructed on a separately rebuilt sample (Appendix B), and not the only nominally significant historical cell (Section 5.6). It carries the qualifications set out in full in Section 6, and its contrast with the baseline results cannot be attributed to exposure timing, since the two samples differ in several respects at once (Section 6.2): a preliminary finding that does not overturn the baseline conclusions. Taken together, the thesis makes two separate contributions in two separate samples (Section 1.5): a side-by-side household/community comparison in the baseline sample, and this preliminary attempt at genuine temporal variation in early-life exposure, which does not extend that comparison, since the historical data cannot separate household from community.

Neither set of results establishes a causal effect of WASH facilities on child outcomes in these four countries, selected for data availability and recency, not to represent Sub-Saharan Africa (Sections 1.4, 6.6), nor a causal policy effect: weak or inconclusive associations do not show WASH investment lacks value, and the conditional associations reported here inform research and interpretation, not policy. The clearest remaining gaps, the historical extension's unresolved measurement documentation and the baseline's exposure-timing limitation, invite future work: validating the Ethiopian interview-date conversion (Appendix C), resolving the weighting question, and tracking the same units across survey rounds (Section 1.2).
